All of the data in this report and the following text is an excerpt from TuSimples original submission (30370-2949-1) and constitutes Navistars sole understanding of this event.
TuSimple's position is that this event does not meet the criteria for reporting under the SGO.
Specifically, the L4 ADS was not in operation at any point in the 30 seconds prior to making contact with the concrete barrier.
The event occurred as follows:
As the truck was being operated on the highway, within its mapped ODD, the driver and test engineer attempted to engage the ADS.
However, the ADS was not functional at that moment due to the computer unit not having been initialized, and should not have been
attempted to be activated. In short, this was a failed attempt to engage the system as a result of human error.
The system has now been modified to prevent the ADS from attempting to engage unless the health of the system is fully functional to
prevent human error from repeating this event.
When the erroneous attempt to engage occurred, the uninitialized vehicle control unit rotated the steering to the left, causing the truck to
veer left. The safety driver took control of the steering, and was able to steer accordingly, but not before the left front truck tire and left
front quarter panel came into contact with the concrete barrier to the left of the lanes of travel.

narrative:
This is a follow up to the e-mail submitted on January 6, 2024, during to the portal maintenance period. This report supplements and clarifies the previous e-mail submission.
The incident occurred about 09:50 PST on Jan [XXX], 2024 near the intersection of [XXX] and [XXX], Las Vegas, NV. There were no injuries reported to Aptiv as a result of the crash involving the subject vehicle.
The subject vehicle with Level 2 ADAS engaged was southbound on [XXX] approaching [XXX].  The subject vehicle was traveling about 30 MPH in the right lane.  An e-scooter was southbound ahead of the subject vehicle in the right turn lane of [XXX] (in the roadway).  The e-scooter then drove into the pedestrian cross-walk from the designated right turning lane, crossed [XXX] and attempted to enter the north/south sidewalk from the roadway.  After entering the sidewalk, the rider of the e-scooter lost control and the rider and e-scooter re-entered the right lane of [XXX]  The rider fell into the road near the curb where he remained, but the e-scooter slid out from under the rider and continued to slide across the roadway until its front wheel reached the middle of the right lane.  The subject vehicle was not involved with nor did it contribute to the rider of the e-scooter losing control or with either the e-scooter or rider re-entering the roadway.
The subject vehicle driver was monitoring the e-scooter and had prepared to react when he noticed the e-scooter attempting to enter the sidewalk.  The subject vehicle driver manually applied the brakes when the e-scooter lost control and entered the roadway from the sidewalk.  The driver's application of the brakes automatically disengaged the Level 2 ADAS system.  The subject vehicle driver also moved left in lane, but was limited by an adjacent vehicle.  The subject vehicle made contact and damaged the front wheel of the e-scooter.  The subject vehicle did not contact the e-scooter rider or any other vehicles at any point.

Torc Robotics and Daimler Truck North America ("DTNA") are submitting duplicate incident reports (refer to Torc report ID: 30330-6882-1) regarding a deer strike involving a Torc-operated vehicle that occurred in Texas on December [XXX], 2023 at 14:35 CST. The vehicle's automated driving system ("ADS") was engaged within 30 seconds prior to the event. Although a deer strike does not appear to meet the SGO's definition of a crash (i.e., impact with a vehicle, other road user, or property), we are reporting this incident out of an abundance of caution and in the interest of transparency. 
At the time of the incident, the vehicle was traveling westbound in the rightmost lane of [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]. A deer crossed the eastbound lanes of traffic and median before entering the westbound lanes.  Torc's in-vehicle fallback test driver ("IFTD"), positioned in the driver's seat, noticed the deer as it entered the westbound lanes. The IFTD took control of the vehicle by disengaging the ADS. The deer then contacted the left side of the tractor. After the physical impact with the tractor, the deer deflected into the left lane toward the left shoulder of the roadway and did not contact other road users. The IFTD reduced the speed of the vehicle and navigated to a rest area to inspect it. During the inspection, the IFTD observed minor damage on the driver's side of the tractor but deemed the vehicle roadworthy for manual operation.  The IFTD contacted local law enforcement to notify them of the event. The test crew (IFTD, safety conductor, and passenger) returned the vehicle to the Torc test operations site.

- The content of this report, including the summary of incident below, is the information as Toyota received from May Mobility on Aug [XXX], 2021.
Summary of incident (as Toyota received from May Mobility):
Leading up to the event, the autonomy system functioned as expected, following the route through the intersection, slowing appropriately for other road users and the red light. Vehicle autonomous behavior was performing as expected and did not require a takeover.
Description of event:
16:17:30 May vehicle, traveling East on [XXX], in full working order with no errors, autonomously navigates the [XXX] and [XXX] intersection.
16:17:35 May vehicle autonomously begins to slow to match the speed of a vehicle several car lengths ahead merging into our lane from the right.
16:17:37 By means of an accelerator pedal push the vehicle is moved into manual mode by the safety operator - from this point forward, the vehicle remains under control of the safety operator.
16:17:43 Manual acceleration command via the pedal increases.
16:17:44 Safety operator manually continues straight which, due to the slight change in angle of the road, brings the May vehicle into contact with the first vehicle to the right.
16:17:44 Safety operator manually applies brake.
16:17:45 With the manual brake command now at maximum the May vehicle makes contact with the second vehicle.
Vehicle indicators for manual or autonomy mode:
The visual indicator for autonomy was functioning properly and as expected in the time leading up to and during the event.
The audio communication device in the vehicle was functioning properly and was used to call for assistance and to report the incident.
The audio beep to indicate a state change was functioning properly.
The safety operator had some audio indication that he had exited autonomy and entered manual operation, and he had full visual indication on his dashboard.

Update Report: 
Toyota completed an assessment of the crash event following review of all currently available data, i.e. field report, PCS FFD, and publicly available map information.  The vehicle was traveling east on [XXX] near the Meadow Vista, CA exit, 1hr 44min into the trip, when the crash event occurred.  In the moments leading up to the crash the vehicle was in an ADAS L2 state, with Lane Tracing Assist (LTA) and Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) functions engaged and travelling at 82mph.  During a left hand curve, the vehicle was centered in the #1 lane (4.65 sec prior to the crash), when the driver induced a steering input (1.7Nm) to the right (3.15 sec prior to the crash).  The vehicle crossed the lane line  into the #2 lane which caused the LTA feature to cancel and disengage (2.40 sec prior to the crash).  The vehicle departed the #2 lane to the right shoulder (1.05 sec prior to the crash).  The vehicle continued drifting to the right without driver steering input before the right side tires exited the pavement and the car pulled to the right, at which the driver applied left steering input (0.30sec).  The vehicle went up the slope to the right side and moved left back into the roadway ending the crash event.  Based on this data, the initial driver input caused the vehicle to exit the lane, which caused the ADAS L2 to disengage, and the driver did not make steering inputs to attempt to regain control of the vehicle until the tires went off the shoulder, 0.30sec prior to the crash.  Also, it was observed that the customer installed a windshield decal (banner style at top) that was partially obstructing the forward camera; this can affect the ability of the camera to recognize lanes.  This is warned against in the owner's manual which states, "Warning: To prevent malfunction of the front camera: do not attach stickers (including transparent stickers) or other items to the area of the windshield in front of the front camera"  (The OM has an illustration of the windshield with shaded area representing area to avoid).  This will be the final update for this incident.

The tail of the tractor trailer scrapped the front passenger panel and the vehicle spun around and moved left across the highway. Guest states the front of the vehicle hit the guard rail and the vehicle stopped in the middle lane. Further, the owners states: "Guest states her son sprained his left wrist. Lane Trace Assist (LTA) was engaged from the start of the recording until approximately 4.8 seconds prior to the collision, and was suspended due to driver steering (EOS torque) over LTA threshold. The vehicle was traveling approximately 78mph leading up to the collision. The steering angle input was steady at -4.5 deg from the beginning of the recording until 0.4 seconds prior to the collision, after which the images show the subject vehicle veering into the lane of the heavy truck, with the steering angle increasing to 31.5 deg at the trigger event. The driver applied the brakes 1.6 seconds after the collision.
The PA State Police Report number that the customer shared was pa24-902406.

On 7/[XXX]/2022 at approximately 3:58 am, a contract test driver was driving a Lucid Air northbound on [XXX] at 70 MPH. The driver reported that he engaged HWA and subsequently fell asleep. When HWA is overridden, it no longer provides lane-keeping and ACC remains active. Approximately 15 seconds later, the vehicle drifted out of its lane and impacted its left side against the roadside barrier on the left side of the road. The driver awoke after the impact and brought the vehicle to a stop on the side of the freeway. Lucid roadside assistance was contacted to tow the vehicle. No airbags deployed. On September 8, 2025, we learned about a single-vehicle collision involving a [XXX] loaner vehicle. The driver alleges that the "driver plus feature" was active and that the vehicle "veered sharply left," causing it to collide with the center median. The vehicle was subsequently towed from the scene. The driver reported visiting an urgent care facility. It is unknown whether he sustained injuries.
Based on available telematics, 33 seconds before the collision, the driver activated ACC. Then, 9 seconds before the collision, he activated Highway Assist. Next, 4 seconds after activating Highway Assist, the driver unbuckled his seatbelt while the vehicle was traveling 62 mph. The driver's actions triggered Highway Assist to disengage and issue audible and visual driver warnings. The driver immediately steered left, and the vehicle struck the center median. The vehicle was traveling at approximately 50 mph at the time of the crash.
Based on the information available, [XXX] believes the driver steering the vehicle left immediately before the impact caused the collision.

The data indicates that the vehicle responded appropriately to all inputs. The driver failing to maintain control of the vehicle was the cause of the collision.

narrative: On October [XXX], 2023, at 2:35 p.m. PST, the subject vehicle was traveling north on [XXX] at approximately 75 mph with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature, Highway Assist (HWA), engaged. While traveling across an overpass at 2:35:18 p.m. PST, HWA disengaged because the subject vehicle moved out of its ODD as a result of insufficient highway markings.  At 2:35:18 p.m. PST, the driver received audio and visual alerts to take over the subject vehicle through in-vehicle messaging. The driver did not heed the warnings and the vehicle began to drift to the right, at which point Lane Keep Assist intervened and guided the vehicle back to the left to avoid crossing over the lane boundary. After this automatic vehicle intervention, the driver finally retook control of the wheel but overcorrected, steering the vehicle to the left until it left the roadway and impacted the side marker at 2:35:21 p.m. PST, causing minor damage to the subject vehicle.

Data indicates that the vehicle did not malfunction and performed as designed in response to driver inputs.

Update: On January [XXX], 2024, at 10:33:20 a.m. PST, the subject vehicle was traveling south on [XXX] at 77 mph with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature, Highway Assist (HWA), engaged. 25 seconds later, at 10:33:45 a.m. the vehicle notified the driver through a message on the driver display that their lane was merging ahead. 19 seconds later, at 10:34:04 a.m. PST, after no intervention from the driver, HWA disengaged because the subject vehicle moved out of its ODD as a result of insufficient highway markings.  At that same time, 10:34:04 a.m., the driver received audio and visual alerts to take over control of the subject vehicle through in-vehicle messaging. At this time the system did not detect hands on the wheel. Less than one second later, at 10:34:05 a.m., the driver put their hands back on the wheel and retook control but input a significant steering angle while still at a high rate of speed (75.4 mph) that started a loss of control. This steering input was not a result of the HWA feature, but an overcorrection by the driver. Over the next nine seconds, from 10:34:05 to 10:34:14 a.m., the driver steered the vehicle to both the left and right trying to regain control, they also applied both the brake and accelerator pedals at various times, sometimes simultaneously, until the vehicle departed the roadway and impacted the side barrier at 10:34:14 a.m. PST, causing damage to the right side of the subject vehicle and deploying the side airbags.

narrative:
On August [XXX], 2024, at approximately 8:01 AM ET the subject vehicle was traveling with adaptive cruise control (ACC) engaged at a speed of approximately 76 mph. ACC is not a level 2 ADAS system, but Rivian is submitting this report because there was some uncertainty in the verbal complaint about whether the driver was allegedly using ACC or Highway Assist (HWA), which is a level 2 feature. The driver initially reported that they were using ACC, but the Rivian call center mistakenly assumed HWA was activated and noted it as such. However, vehicle telematics data demonstrates that HWA was not active during the crash or in the 30 seconds prior to this crash and that ACC was the system in use leading up to the crash.
The verbal report from the driver was difficult to understand but Rivians takeaway from the incident is that the vehicle was in the left lane with ACC activated when the lane ended. The driver admitted that they did not react to the lane ending in time and the vehicle impacted the center divider with the side of the vehicle. Damage to the vehicle is unknown but the customer reported that the airbags deployed and that the vehicle had to be towed.

The vehicle's automated driving system ("ADS") was engaged within 30 seconds prior to the event. Although a deer strike does not appear to meet the SGO's definition of a crash (i.e., impact with a vehicle, other road user, or property), we are reporting this incident out of an abundance of caution and in the interest of transparency. 
At the time of the incident, the vehicle was traveling westbound in the rightmost lane of [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]. A deer crossed the eastbound lanes of traffic and median before entering the westbound lanes.  Torc's in-vehicle fallback test driver ("IFTD"), positioned in the driver's seat, noticed the deer as it entered the westbound lanes. The IFTD took control of the vehicle by disengaging the ADS. The deer then contacted the left side of the tractor. After the physical impact with the tractor, the deer deflected into the left lane toward the left shoulder of the roadway and did not contact other road users. narrative:
TuSimple's position is that this event does not meet the criteria for reporting under the SGO.
Specifically, the L4 ADS was not in operation at any point in the 30 seconds prior to making contact with the concrete barrier.  
 
The event occurred as follows:
As the truck was being operated on the highway, within its mapped ODD, the driver and test engineer attempted to engage the ADS.  However, the ADS was not functional at that moment due to the computer unit not having been initialized, and should not have been attempted to be activated.  In short, this was a failed attempt to engage the system as a result of human error.  
 
The system has now been modified to prevent the ADS from attempting to engage unless the health of the system is fully functional to prevent human error from repeating this event.
 
When the erroneous attempt to engage occurred, the uninitialized vehicle control unit rotated the steering to the left, causing the truck to veer left.  The safety driver took control of the steering, and was able to steer accordingly, but not before the left front truck tire and left front quarter panel came into contact with the concrete barrier to the left of the lanes of travel.  
 
The contact resulted in a scuff to the left tire and damage to the radar unit extending from the left quarter panel.

During normal autonomous operation, the May autonomous shuttle (Ego) was traveling through a narrow section of roadway in a parking lot bordered by parked vehicles on the left and a retaining wall on the right on experimental software version v29.0.20. As the Ego proceeded, the system initially recognized the static retaining wall as a large, non-rectangular object. As the Ego approaches the wall, the resulting density of lidar returns on the object (wall) exceeds the detectors maximum limitation. The newer lidar points, toward the forward edge of the elongated object, exceeding the limit were filtered out, causing the track to disappear when the ego approached 5m from the track (i.e. the wall). The situation was exacerbated by the fact that the road edge was incorrectly marked in that section.  The road edge was drawn through the retaining wall and thus the vehicle did not have any prior knowledge about the edge of the road. As a result, the Ego drove too close to the wall, scraping it at a speed of 2 meters per second while driving straight (i.e. in lane-nominal policy) with no nudge or veer corrections. There was no damage to the wall. The limitation leading to the lost track affects Software versions v26.0 (when the Open World Tracklet v2 feature was introduced) through v31.0. This is the only known instance of this failure mode, and in v32.0 an optimization was made to remove the LIDAR threshold entirely and mitigate the vulnerability.  Furthermore, the incorrect road edge annotation was corrected shortly after this incident and the map updated for the deployed vehicles.

narrative:
The May vehicle was traveling on an unpainted (no center line) residential road with vehicles parked along the right side of the road. The May vehicle passed too close to a parked vehicle, causing the May vehicle's passenger-side mirror to contact the parked vehicle's driver-side mirror.
The May vehicle's ground mapping module had fallen significantly behind in its processing of lidar data. As a result, actual objects were being filtered out of the lidar data during object detection. This filtering caused the truck to oscillate between being detected, detecting only the cab, detecting the cab and mirror, and not being detected at all.
After assessing the issue, it has been determined that ground map latency alone will not cause safety issues. There is no risk to VRUs, or anything at ground level. The issue was with something in the air (mirror), above the ground.
A permanent fix to address the ground map latency issue is in process and will be implemented in the entire fleet within the next 30 days.
The second factor in the collision is that we were artificially constraining the vehicle to the right side of the road due to ambiguous and unpainted roadway. If we change that constraint to an advisory line (and allow the vehicle to cross the line to the left), we would have been far enough to the left to avoid collision (simulation success).
Solution Implementation: AVO training for extra caution related to protruding items like mirrors (short term), software changes coming in the next update and hotfix (within 30 days), and further improvement in the following update (within 60 days).
Until the tested software changes are implemented, we have advised the AVOs to take extra caution in these scenarios and to continue to disengage autonomy when desired. As always, we sacrifice autonomy for safety, as needed.

While traveling northbound on[XXX] in Martinez, a car pulled out of a driveway on the right side without right of way and collided with the right side of May's vehicle (t-bone.)
May's vehicle was traveling at approximately 20 MPH in a residential neighborhood, and was approximately 1m left of lane center when a black vehicle exited a driveway on the right from behind a fence, facing the road and May's vehicle. This vehicle did not slow down or stop until entering into the roadway and collided with the May vehicle's right side. AVO attempts to swerve to the left but is unable to avoid a collision.

The velocity of the other vehicle was underestimated and was largely given only yield policies as having the most significant likelihood. There is some room for improvement in our response, which we plan to implement in future software releases, namely, an emergency veer policy must exist that is capable of moving quickly and far enough to possibly avoid the collision, more accurate reporting of velocity for slow-moving agents, estimate acceleration when assessing risk, improvements to predictions of the probability of an agent yielding, and adjusting our risk assessment so that it is heading dependent and more risk would be associated with passing close in front of another vehicle.

The May vehicle was involved in a rear-end collision shortly after completing a right-hand turn. As the vehicle proceeded through its turn, it encountered exhaust fumes from vehicles waiting at a stoplight in the adjacent lane. Due to environmental conditions and sensor limitations, the vehicle's lidar system interpreted the exhaust plume as a solid object in its path. In response, the autonomous vehicle first tried to adjust its position. When this maneuver proved insufficient, the system initiated a hard stop response. The vehicle behind, which was following at approximately 7-8 meters, was unable to stop in time and collided with the rear of the autonomous vehicle. The collision occurred at relatively low speeds (the autonomous vehicle had decelerated from approximately 7.6 m/s to 0 m/s), though exact impact speeds of the following vehicle were not recorded. The primary factor that led to this incident is that Lidar does not pierce through exhaust so the exhaust cloud appears to be a large, solid object. Some corrective actions that will be implemented: consider weather implication in future platform sensor selection and continue working on the software to improve a neural network to classify lidar points, which will use temporal information, radar, and camera features to make a decision on whether a lidar point is truly an object.

A May shuttle began a test shift on experimental software in a parking sub-lot. The vehicle exited the sub-lot and rolled over a curb. The vehicle stopped at a stop sign at the exit of the main lot. As it proceeded to turn onto the main road, it rolled over another curb. Almost immediately after rolling the curb, the vehicle began to drift right in lane, rubbing the vehicle sidewall on a curb. The test driver intervened immediately, but not before the sidewall of the rear right tire was weakened. Later during the drive while under manual control, the sidewall fails, eventually leading to a low pressure indicator illuminating in the dash. It was discovered that the deployment of map files, which must remain compatible, was incomplete, leaving a mismatch in the system. This resulted in the vehicle having an incorrect estimate of where lanes are in the coordinates of our localization map, and as a result, the vehicle had an incorrect estimate of proximity to lane boundaries, resulting in curb strikes.

narrative:
A Ghost ADS-equipped car was driving engaged Northbound on [XXX]. As always, there were two safety drivers in the car. Traffic was moving in all four lanes at or near the speed limit. The Ghost vehicle was in the right-middle lane. Another vehicle (the "lead" car) entered into the Ghost car's lane from the right. While there were numerous vehicles ahead of the Ghost car before that vehicle entered the lane, the lead vehicle blocked the view of the lane before it. Throughout the incident, traffic in the other three lanes continued at a steady pace.
When the lead vehicle entered into the lane ahead of the Ghost car, the Ghost car applied the brakes to accommodate the intrusion and then continued to match the speed of the lead car. The lead car suddenly slammed the brakes. The Ghost car followed suit, reducing its speed from 19 mps (42.5 mph) to 4.7 mps (10.5 mph) within the next three seconds. The Ghost car was able to match the rapid speed reduction of the lead car and avoid contact.
The driver following the Ghost car was not able to respond as quickly as the Ghost ADS. When the following driver began to apply the brakes, the car was about five meters behind and was traveling at 6.5 mps. At the point of impact, the Ghost vehicle was traveling at 4.78 mps (10.7 mph), matching the lead car. There were no injuries. The vehicles suffered only cosmetic damage, the drivers exchanged information, and the Ghost safety drivers returned to home base in conventional mode.

On June [XXX], 2025, a Beep-operated Ford E-Transit (004D) equipped with an automated driving system developed by Oxa Autonomy Ltd. was involved in a collision with a third-party vehicle in Jacksonville, FL. 
While navigating northbound on [XXX], vehicle 004D approached the intersection of [XXX] under automated control. As vehicle 004D proceeded through the intersection, a 2020 Nissan Pathfinder navigating eastbound on [XXX] entered the intersection and struck vehicle 004D on the drivers door. Vehicle 004D had right of way through the intersection with no stop or yield the other vehicle had been stopped at a stop sign prior to the collision. There were no injuries reported at the scene, and both vehicles were driven away from the site of the collision. 
Prior to the collision, the safety operator in vehicle 004D stated that they noticed the other vehicle entering the intersection, applied the vehicles brakes, and steered away from the path of the other vehicle. Though they were able to bring vehicle 004D to a complete stop, they were unable to completely avoid the collision. Review of dashcam footage and of CCTV footage covering the intersection corroborate this narrative. The safety operator was referred for a post-accident drug and alcohol testing after the incident. They tested negative for any impairment. 
Analysis of the ADS logs determined that the ADS had detected the potential collision and had planned an emergency braking action. The safety operators intervention revoked control of the vehicle from the ADS preventing any automated braking actions. 
The [XXX] responded to the accident scene. The driver of the other vehicle was cited for failing to stop at the stop sign, and the JSO CSO noted that vehicle 004D was not at fault for the accident.

On August [XXX], 2025, a Beep-operated Ford E-Transit (002B) equipped with an automated driving system developed by Oxa Autonomy Ltd. was involved in a collision with a stationary object in Jacksonville, FL.
While navigating westbound on [XXX] along a predefined route, vehicle 002B began to slowly veer towards the right curb. The vehicle eventually climbed the curb with the right front and rear wheels and the passenger-side mirror contacted a stationary light pole.
There was one passenger onboard at the time of the incident, an employee of the Jacksonville Transportation Authority. There were no reported injuries, and the vehicle was driven from the scene.
Review of the automated driving system logs as well as onboard video footage determined that the operator disengaged the automated driving system 7.5 seconds prior to the vehicle mounting the curb. Further examination of the onboard video footage noted that the operator appeared to be drowsy and inattentive prior to the incident.
Beep confirmed that the operators shift was in compliance with anti-fatigue policies for this operation. The operator was referred for a post-accident drug and alcohol testing following the incident and tested negative for any impairment. Following the conclusion of the investigation into this incident, the operator was separated from employment.

While navigating eastbound on [XXX], vehicle 003C was struck on the driver-side rear quarter panel by a 2020 Toyota Prius performing an illegal U-turn from the opposing lane. On January [XXX], 2026, a Beep-operated Karsan EJEST (BEEP-EJEST-0001) equipped with an automated driving system (ADS) develop by ADASTEC Corporation (ADASTEC) was involved in a collision with a third-party vehicle in Washington, D.C.

While traveling in autonomous mode westbound on [XXX] in the left-hand lane, the vehicle encountered a double-parked vehicle partially intruded into BEEP-EJEST-0001's lane of travel. BEEP-EJEST-0001 began to slow from its planned speed, and as decelerated, a human-driven Tesla Model Y (VEHICLE2) traveling parallel to BEEP-EJEST-0001 in the right-hand lane attempted to pull behind BEEP-EJEST-0001 to pass the double-parked vehicle in its lane of travel. Available data indicated that VEHICLE2 followed BEEP-EJEST-0001 at a distance insufficient to respond to rapid deceleration and initiated a lane transition across a solid lane line immediately prior to contact.

narrative:
On December [XXX], 2022, a Navya ARMA shuttle operated by Beep (VIN 1N9A1SACXJS[XXX]) was involved in a non-injury collision while operating in manual mode on [XXX] in Port Saint Lucie, FL.  While driving along [XXX] under autonomous control, the shuttle encountered a parked vehicle partially blocking its path, requiring disengagement of the autonomous drive system.  The safety driver attempted to manually drive the shuttle around the parked vehicle to reengage the autonomous drive system.  While manually steering the shuttle around the parked vehicle blocking its path, the shuttle failed to respond to manual control input and steered to the left, impacting a parked vehicle at a low rate of speed on the opposite side of [XXX].  The six passengers onboard alighted the shuttle, an accident report was filed with the local police, and the shuttle was removed from the scene.  Initial reports from the onboard safety driver indicated that while steering around the vehicle blocking the shuttle's path, the shuttle became unresponsive to control input.  The safety driver released the operator present button on the vehicle controller, which serves as dead man switch however, the vehicle failed to stop.  After the incident, further investigation by Navya confirmed that the root cause of the incident was a failure of the Xbox 360 controller used to manually control the vehicle.  Contact with the parked vehicle occurred between the time of failure and the vehicle drive system recognizing that the controller had failed an elapsed time of 4.05 seconds. In response to the incident, Beep suspended operation of all Navya ARMA vehicles pending identification and implementation of appropriate solutions to mitigate the risk of this failure leading to future incidents.
Subsequent investigation by Beep and Navya determined that the vehicle control software, NavyaDrive, is limited in its ability to monitor the validity of control signal input received from the Xbox 360 controller.  As the safety driver began to manually steer the vehicle, the controller failed, sending constant turning input to the vehicle drive system leading to the collision.  Though Navya developed software mitigations due to prior issues encountered with the controller, those mitigations were ineffective with respect to the failure leading to the incident on December [XXX].  Further, due to the short time between the controller failing and the collision (2.34sec), the safety driver was unable to identify the controller failure and trigger the emergency stop before the collision occurred.
In response to the incident, Navya is integrating a revised manual control system on the ARMA shuttle platform.  The revised manual control system utilizes industrial-grade components for improved electromechanical reliability and allows for active monitoring of the control system health, eliminating the root cause of the failure that led to the incident on December [XXX].  Software upgrades of all Navya ARMA vehicles will further reintroduce automated braking function while the ARMA vehicle is under manual control.  Beep is working with Navya to retrofit its fleet of ARMA vehicles with the revised manual control system as well as retrain and recertify its safety driver staff on the updated NavyaDrive software.
Discussion of the root cause analysis and solution design for the revised manual control system will be provided to NHTSA as a supplement to this report.

VIN # VG9A2CB2CIV[XXX] 
At approximately 5:54 p.m. on Wednesday, August [XXX], 2023, P84, travelling eastbound on [XXX], approached the three-way stop at [XXX] and [XXX]. P84 arrived at the intersection at the same time as two other vehicles: a grey van heading northbound on [XXX] and a red sedan heading westbound on [XXX]. The safety driver yielded to the northbound vehicle, which proceeded to make a right-hand turn eastbound onto [XXX]. After allowing the intersection to clear, the safety driver onboard P84 confirmed that it was safe for the shuttle to proceed through the intersection. As the shuttle entered the intersection, a second vehicle travelling northbound on [XXX], a white sedan, entered the intersection intending a left-hand turn onto westbound [XXX]. Both vehicles entered the intersection simultaneously, subsequently colliding at a low rate of speed in the middle of the intersection.  
At approximately 5:57 p.m., the Beep Command Center (BCC) was informed by the safety driver that P84 was involved in a minor collision with another vehicle at the intersection of [XXX] and [XXX]. The incident response protocol was initiated, and a supervisor dispatched to the scene. Local law enforcement (San Francisco Police Department) was contacted to report the collision but declined to respond given the minor nature of the collision, directing both parties to exchange information. After the Beep supervisor arrived on scene at approximately 6:49 p.m., the safety driver and supervisor removed the shuttle from the roadway and exchanged insurance information with the driver of the other vehicle. 
Damage to both vehicles was noted to be very minor. The shuttle sustained light scuffs, chips, and small paint transfer. The other vehicle sustained a small dent on the fender. Neither vehicle required towing, and both were safely driven from the scene. 
Beeps safety driver was subsequently subjected to a standard post-collision drug & alcohol screening which has since cleared.  
Contributing Factors 
Based on an analysis of the available evidence, Beep has determined the following factors may have contributed to the higher likelihood of a collision occurring in this instance: 
1.The white sedan failed to yield to P84 in accordance with California state law governing intersection priority.
2.The slight bend in P84s path to accommodate the lane shift through the intersection may have reduced the available stopping distance as the white sedan was not perceived as an obstacle in P84s path until it proceeded further into the intersection.
Incident Findings 
Beep developed the following findings regarding this incident:
1.P84 behaved as expected, detecting and maintaining awareness of the white sedan in the moments preceding the collision, commanding hard braking maneuver, and achieving a 3m/s2 deceleration rate once the white sedan encroached on P84s path.
2.The safety driver observed California state law and had the right of way when releasing P84 into the intersection.
3.The safety driver could have avoided the collision by using the emergency stop. The safety driver indicated that they were aware of the other vehicle through the duration of the incident and were aware of the proper procedure in this scenario but panicked in the moment.
Mitigation:
Implement a priority zone to account for the slight bend in the shuttles path and for future vehicles that may fail to yield.

At Approximately 12:39 PM, the Beep Command Center (BCC) informed the LYNX dispatch center that another autonomous shuttle operating on the same route (VIN: VG9A2CB2CJV[XXX]) was being taken out of service due to insufficient battery charge to continue operation. The BCC later informed LYNX dispatch at 12:49PM that the second shuttle operating on route, P131, would also be returning to storage after the operator completed its current loop. At Approximately 12:52 PM, P131 approached the [XXX] stop within the designated Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) operating lane. The shuttle remained stopped for approximately two (2) and a half minutes while three (3) passengers alighted, and two (2) additional passengers boarded the shuttle. During that period, approximately two (2) minutes after stopping to service passengers, a LYNX bus pulled behind P131. Approximately thirty (30) seconds later, the LYNX bus exited the BRT lane and proceeded into the public travel lane alongside the BRT lane. As the LYNX bus entered the public travel lane, the safety driver onboard P131 engaged the autonomous drive system, and the shuttle proceeded in the BRT lane. After both vehicles had begun moving, P131 in the BRT lane and the LYNX bus in the public travel lane, the LYNX bus reentered the BRT lane encroaching on the shuttles path. The bus failed to provide adequate clearance and contacted the left front side of P131. Both vehicles stopped in the BRT lane after the collision. 
Within five (5) minutes of the collision, all passengers had safely alighted from the shuttle with no reported injuries and left the scene without giving statements. At approximately 2:20PM, the City of Orlando Police Department (OPD) arrived on scene to investigate the incident. Beep and LYNX supervisors were on scene to support the investigation. OPD collected statements from both the Beep safety driver and LYNX bus driver. The LYNX supervisor provided OPD access to the LYNX bus camera footage on scene, at which point the investigating officer made a verbal indication that the LYNX bus driver appeared to be at fault for the collision. 
Beeps safety driver was subsequently subjected to a standard post-collision drug and alcohol screening. 
1.The safety driver did not exhibit complete situational awareness and per their after-incident interview, failed to notice the bus prior to departing the station. Had the attendant continued to look and check behind/alongside P131 prior to departing the station,
the collision may have been avoided.
2.The safety driver attempted to stop the shuttle by disengaging the ADS using the HMI rather than using the emergency stop button. Use of the emergency stop would have increased the deceleration rate to 5 m/s2, decreasing the stopping distance of the shuttle. However, it is not clear whether use of the emergency stop would have fully avoided the collision given the point at which the LYNX LYMMO bus entered the BRT lane.

narrative:
This incident occurred near Ranger, TX on [XXX] at approximately 9:56 am CT on Nov. [XXX], 2023. The Aurora vehicle was operating in autonomy at the time. Conditions were overcast, with light rain. As the Aurora vehicle was driving in its lane at 67 mph, a Ford pick-up truck overtaking the Aurora vehicle in the rightmost lane at approximately 80 mph appears to have hydroplaned, lost control, and hit the passenger-side rear portion of the trailer. Before the collision, the Aurora Driver detected the pick-up trucks encroachment into the Aurora vehicles lane and initiated a nudge to the left to provide space. This was insufficient to completely avoid the collision, and the pick-up truck made contact with the passenger side rear of the trailer. The Aurora Driver detected the collision and made the decision to initiate an incident response, but before it could execute that response, the Vehicle Operator took over control of the system and proceeded in manual. The Vehicle Operator received the notification that a collision had been detected and was initiating an incident response. The Vehicle Operator did not visually observe the collision and therefore assumed the reaction of the Aurora Driver to be a software anomaly worth escalated attention, rather than the correct detection of a collision and thus reported the incident through our escalated annotation protocol, rather than through our incident response protocols. We identified the incident at approximately 8:45 am CT on December [XXX], 2023, through a review of our data logs. 
At this time, we are not aware of any injuries and, from camera footage, the pick-up truck also appears to have left the scene of the incident. There is also no indication of any cargo or major trailer damage.

narrative:
This incident occurred near Streetman, TX on [XXX] at approximately 3:03 PM CT on February [XXX], 2024. The Aurora vehicle was operating in autonomy at the time. Conditions were clear. As the Aurora vehicle was driving in its lane at 62 mph, a box truck veered into the lane of the Aurora vehicle. The box truck's mirror appeared to make contact with the back of the trailer that the Aurora Driver was pulling. At this time, we are not aware of any injuries, and camera footage appears to show that the box truck continued to drive. From the post-trip inspection, there was not any visible trailer damage. 
Before the collision, the Aurora Driver was driving straight in its lane and passing the box truck. Shortly thereafter, the box truck began to encroach into the lane of the Aurora Driver. The Aurora Driver detected the box truck's encroachment into the Aurora vehicle's lane and initiated a nudge away from the box truck to provide space. The Aurora Driver detected the collision and made the decision to initiate an incident response, but before it could execute that response, the Vehicle Operator took over control of the system and proceeded in manual. The Aurora vehicle then re-engaged in autonomy approximately two minutes later. 
The Vehicle Operator did not visually observe the collision, assumed the reaction of the Aurora Driver to be a software anomaly, and reported the vehicle nudge through our standard annotation protocol rather than through our incident response protocols. We identified the incident at approximately 1:03 PM CT on February [XXX], 2024 through a review of our data logs.

narrative:
On May [XXX], 2025, a Plus autonomous test truck was driving in autonomous mode on a public highway in Texas with a Safety Driver.  Plus's safety drivers are experienced and well-trained. The Safety Driver operating the particular vehicle has 12-years of over-the-road commercial vehicle driving experience. All safety drivers are trained to manage potential hazards they may encounter on the roads and are encouraged to retake control of the vehicle whenever necessary to ensure safe operation.  
Here, the Plus vehicle was traveling Northbound on [XXX] at approximately 63 mph in mild to moderate traffic with clear weather conditions.  According to the video camera log, the truck was in autonomous mode when a black SUV traveling in the right-most driving lane swerved to the right into the emergency lane (i.e., the shoulder) to avoid a vehicle that had stopped before it in the driving lane. Seeing the disabled vehicle in the driving lane, the Plus Safety Driver took control of the truck by applying the brakes and began to decelerate the vehicle. Two vehicles traveling behind the black SUV in the same lane then swerved to the left and into the lane in which the Plus vehicle was traveling.  The left side of the second of these vehicles (a minivan) made contact with the Plus truck's right side. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]
The Plus truck swerved slightly into the lane to its left as a result of the contact, avoiding a pickup truck that was passing by it. The Safety Driver then re-centered the vehicle into the truck's original lane. After the contact, the minivan moved into the rightmost lane and then ultimately came to a stop in the emergency lane.  The Plus Safety Driver changed lanes and also brought the truck to a stop in the emergency lane.
A Police report was taken at the scene, but the Plus Safety Driver did not receive a copy of it.  Based on our best information, none of the passengers in the minivan reported injuries and the only damage was to the vehicle's driver-side tire.  The minivan nevertheless was towed away from the scene.  The Plus truck did not have any damage and was able to continue driving to its destination.

narrative:
On January [XXX], 2023, RRAI received a support request through their Customer Support Portal from Beep, Inc., the owner of the vehicle, regarding their Olli 2.0 vehicle bumping into the curb in Peachtree Corners, GA. At 11:01 am, while running the normal route, the Olli contacted the adjacent curb on the front right side, causing tie rod and cosmetic damage. No one was injured and the only damage was to the vehicle itself. The customer contacted RRAI through the client support portal shortly after the incident. No injuries occurred, there were no passengers besides the safety operator, no other vehicles were involved, and no emergency systems were engaged.
Olli 2.0 (S/N 2-18) is an 8-passenger shuttle that is no longer manufactured. The vehicle manufacturer, Local Motors, dissolved in 2022. Local Motors contracted RRAI to install autonomy kits for several Olli shuttles during the period of 2018 - 2020. RRAI provided some support for initial site deployment and ensured customer safety operators were trained on the autonomy system. Since the Local Motors dissolution in 2022, almost all Olli vehicles have been decommissioned.
To date, we have concluded the following:
1. There were no updates or alterations made by RRAI in the months prior to Jan [XXX]. In previous operations, including the immediately preceding operations on January 20th, 2023, Olli 2-18 ran the route as normal with no anomalies. There were no software updates or other system changes before it was run again on January [XXX], 2023, the date of curb contact.
2. The root cause of the curb contact was a communication error with the HD Map registration module. HD Map registration utilizes real-time lidar and positioning data and compares that to a-priori HD maps stored within the autonomy system. A communication problem occurred between the computer running the map registration software and the computer running the navigation algorithms. The cause for the communication problem has been identified and a fix has been implemented to prevent the issue from happening again (see below).
3. Steering was out of calibration. It was noted through data collection that the steering was out of calibration at time of incident. The autonomy system was attempting to correct this issue, but the vehicular steering system could not achieve the required turn radius. This is a vehicular maintenance concern managed by the customer.
It was determined that the HD map registration issue had not been observed during autonomous operations in the previous four years. The solution to prevent further occurrences includes:
1. Implementing a self-diagnostic routine upon system boot, which ensures the communication connection is established. If the connection is not established, this diagnostic will prevent the vehicle from driving autonomously. 
2. Updating the error checks to ensure that during run time, the vehicle will come to a controlled stop in event of a communication problem.  
3. Working with the customer to recalibrate the steering, and assisting in reviewing customer's vehicle maintenance checks for steering calibration if necessary.
4. Continuing to review data to determine other concerns or improvements.

narrative: The vehicle in front of the customer's vehicle slowed down abruptly on the freeway and the customer immediately stepped on the brake to slow her vehicle down. The customer's vehicle slowed down in a straight line without locking-up of the wheels, indicating ABS worked as intended. The customer's vehicle was then rear-ended by the vehicle which was unable to stop resulting in a minor fender-bender on the freeway. No injuries were reported and both vehicles sustained only scratches and were able to drive away from the scene.

The customer was traveling on a two lane, country road, which was missing lane markings on the sides of the road - only the middle line was properly marked. The speed limit on the country road is 35MPH. The customer noticed a pothole on the side of the road, swerved towards the middle of the road to avoid it, but the LKA assist engaged and moved the vehicle back in the lane. By doing so, the vehicle ran over the pothole, with both front and back passenger side tires and damaged both wheel and tires in the process. During our investigation, we determined that in this case the LKA worked as intended. The system is designed to prioritize a solid line, and can't detect a pothole, and since the road is very narrow (our estimate is less than 3m per side) the vehicle unfortunately ran over the pothole. LKA/ELK system limitations throughout the industry are similar: the LKA/ELK systems try to keep vehicle inside the lane, to prevent a vehicle from drifting out, and the system can't predict driver intention, for example: Is the driver crossing solid lane intentionally or by accident, is hard to distinguish. Relevant override conditions in this case are:
- Steering wheel speed  200deg/s
- Steering torque  3.5Nm
In our application, the override force is limited by the EU homologation test and therefore, we feel that the vehicle behaved as expected and should have been over-powered by the driver to avoid the pothole, thus eliminating a costly replacement cost of two wheels and tires.

On December [XXX], 2025, Ford received notification of an incident, involving an 2025 F-150.  The incident occurred on December [XXX], 2025. According to the driver's account, the vehicle was traveling northbound on [XXX], occupying the leftmost lane of a three-lane highway.  The driver reported that BlueCruise was engaged at the time. 
As the F-150 approached the on-ramp leading to [XXX], the driver observed that the vehicle immediately ahead had abruptly changed lanes to avoid stopped traffic. The driver stated that he took manual control of the vehicle, applied the brakes, and steered into the center lane.  While executing this maneuver, the F-150 was struck from behind by a trailing vehicle.  The impact propelled the F-150 forward, resulting in a second collision with the vehicle in front of the F-150. 

The F-150 driver reported that the driver of the vehicle that rear-ended the F-150 experienced an airbag deployment, sustained injuries, and was transported to the hospital. No other injuries or airbag deployments were reported as a result of the incident. 

Given the F-150 driver's assertion that BlueCruise was active prior to the incident, Ford conducted a search for connected vehicle data associated with the event.  Ford's analysis of this data confirms that ADAS L2 (BlueCruise) was engaged within 30 seconds before the collision and that BlueCruise disengaged when the driver pressed the brakes, approximately seven seconds before the F-150 was rear-ended.

Monthly update on report [XXX] (reported on Feb [XXX], 2026):
Ford obtained the police report relating to this incident. According to the police report, the driver stated that, while utilizing the hands-free driving system, he took his eyes off the road and reached into the rear of the vehicle to retrieve a hat. While the driver was reaching into the rear of the vehicle, it drifted left toward the guardrail. The driver attempted to correct but lost control, crashing into the guardrail. 

Ford also obtained physical access to the vehicle and was able to extract EDR data from the Restraints Control Module. This data shows: 1) that the vehicle was traveling at a pre-collision speed of 69 mph; 2) that approximately one second prior to impacting the barrier the steering wheel angle registered a leftward input of 40 degrees; and 3) that this leftward steering input occurred rapidly, in less than half a second. This extreme (40 degrees) and rapid (<0.5 second) steering angle change at high vehicle speed (69 mph) far exceeds the steering input capabilities of the BlueCruise system. 

The police report and the EDR data therefore confirm that the incident was caused by abrupt manual steering wheel input, most likely from inadvertent contact with the steering wheel while the driver was turning and reaching into the rear of the vehicle.

narrative: This single-vehicle crash involved a 2019 Cadillac CT6 that hit a highway median. GM's current understanding of the crash is based on OnStar telematics data and the driver's statements after the crash to an OnStar representative.  Before the crash, the vehicle was proceeding on a highway road with Super Cruise engaged at 70 mph at 09:41:21.  According to the OnStar audio recordings, the driver stated that his knee contacted the steering wheel causing the vehicle to veer left and crash into the highway median.  Telematics data indicates that the vehicle was in Super Cruise "active" mode when the steering wheel was manually moved and the vehicle entered a manual override mode 7 seconds prior to the crash.  According to the AACN report, airbags were not deployed and the driver was not buckled.  According to the OnStar Audio recording the driver hit his head on the roof rail and commented that his back hurt and may need an x-ray, however, it is unknown if the driver sought medical attention at a hospital. Contact to the local police station confirmed the vehicle was towed.

Customer stated that she suffered bruises and friction burns from the airbags deploying and requested that Kia pay her vehicle loan and provide with a new vehicle.  
The subject Kia EV6 is equipped with HDA, LFA and SCC. HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. The driver is responsible for controlling the vehicle for safe driving as HDA is not an autonomous driving system.  In addition, HDA may not be able to recognize all traffic situations and may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system.  LFA is also a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road, and assists the drivers steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. LFA does not operate at all times and it is the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle and to maintain the vehicle in its lane.  
Kia has reached out to the customer and left several messages via phone and email in an effort to obtain authorization to retrieve the ACU and download the EDR data for its investigation into the customers allegations. 9/13/2024 Update to 855-8237-2:
MBUSA conducted a scene and vehicle inspection on August 14, 2024, which included a physical examination of the vehicle. The subject vehicle was located in a salvage yard. The subject vehicle was left uncovered, exposing the vehicle to rain and other weather conditions (including heavy rains associated with Tropical Storm Debby). A significant amount of standing water was observed in both the driver and passenger footwells. As a result of this water damage to the subject vehicle, MBUSA was not able to establish a connection to the vehicle system diagnostics, control units, or EDR. 
A physical inspection of the braking and steering systems was subsequently performed. This inspection did not identify evidence of any steering or braking malfunction and the available information indicates both systems operated as intended at the time of the incident. The dashcam videos provided by the owner show the driver increasing the vehicles speed from 35mph at the start of the video to 46.5mph at the time of the crash. No audible warnings or steering wheel movement were observed in the driver-facing video. When DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist is active, the vehicle is designed to allow a driver to overrule and suppress the system by depressing the accelerator pedal. Based on the speed increase observed in the provided videos, it suggests that the system was not providing speed control to the subject vehicle prior to the incident.
Based on its investigation and review of the videos provided by the vehicle owner, MBUSA has concluded that that the vehicle operated as intended and that DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist was likely not engaged during the 24-second period captured by the dashcam video recording and when the driver lost consciousness. MBUSA has concluded its investigation into this matter.

Reference: Aurora Operations, Inc. NHTSA-Provided Report # 30530-6818-1
This incident occurred near Ranger, TX on [XXX]  approximately 9:56 am CT on November [XXX], 2023. The Aurora vehicle was operating in autonomy at the time. Conditions were overcast, with light rain. As the Aurora vehicle was driving in its lane at 67 mph, a Ford pick-up truck overtaking the Aurora vehicle in the rightmost lane at approximately 80 mph appears to have hydroplaned, lost control, and hit the passenger-side rear portion of the trailer. 
Before the collision, the Aurora Driver detected the pick-up truck's encroachment into the Aurora vehicle's lane and initiated a nudge to the left to provide space. This was insufficient to completely avoid the collision, and the pickup truck made contact with the passenger side rear of the trailer. The Aurora Driver detected the collision and made the decision to initiate an incident response, but before it could execute that response, the Vehicle Operator took over control of the system and proceeded in manual. The Vehicle Operator received the notification that a collision had been detected and was initiating an incident response. The Vehicle Operator did not visually observe the collision and therefore assumed the reaction of the Aurora Driver to be a software anomaly worth escalated attention, rather than the correct detection of a collision and thus reported the incident through our escalated annotation protocol, rather than through our incident response protocols. We identified the incident at approximately 8:45 am CT on December [XXX], 2023 through a review of our data logs.
At this time, we are not aware of any injuries and, from camera footage, the pick-up truck also appears to have left the scene of the incident. There is also no indication of any cargo or major trailer damage.

narrative:
This incident occurred near Streetman, TX on [XXX] at approximately 3:03 PM CT on February [XXX], 2024. The Aurora vehicle was operating in autonomy at the time. Conditions were clear. As the Aurora vehicle was driving in its lane at 62 mph, a box truck veered into the lane of the Aurora vehicle. The box truck's mirror appeared to make contact with the back of the trailer that the Aurora Driver was pulling. At this time, we are not aware of any injuries, and camera footage appears to show that the box truck continued to drive. From the post-trip inspection, there was not any visible trailer damage. Before the collision, the Aurora Driver was driving straight in its lane and passing the box truck. Shortly thereafter, the box truck began to encroach into the lane of the Aurora Driver. The Aurora Driver detected the box truck's encroachment into the Aurora vehicle's lane and initiated a nudge away from the box truck to provide space. The Aurora Driver detected the collision and made the decision to initiate an incident response, but before it could execute that response, the Vehicle Operator took over control of the system and proceeded in manual. The Aurora vehicle then re-engaged in autonomy approximately two minutes later. 
The Vehicle Operator did not visually observe the collision, assumed the reaction of the Aurora Driver to be a software anomaly, and reported the vehicle nudge through the standard annotation protocol rather than through the incident response protocols. The incident was identified at approximately 1:03 PM CT on February 2, 2024, through a review of Aurora's data logs.
